en: Have you twisted my words
And grieved me so, Kyyaz.
If you do not seize as spoil
The impetuous woman Chürök,
And return boasting
To your Seven Rivers, your land of Tarkan,
Saying, ‘I raised a tumult
Over Chürök, for whom Toltoy died;
I took the woman as spoil;
I avenged the old grievance,
The ancient rancor of brave Toltoy,’
If you cannot boast of that,
What sort of khan are you among the Kazakhs?
Where is the spirit in you
That sustains a people and keeps a nation?
You smashed her gate with axes,
And took her gold into your sacks;
You made the red-robed, slender-waisted
Maiden your spoil.
Yet when you met her face to face,
You grew terrified of Aichürök
And started a quarrel, wretched Kyyaz.
You took the renowned land of Talas,
Took the Argyn and Kyrgyz peoples,
Took Külchoro and giant Bakay,
And took countless thoroughbred herds.
The many champions who entered combat,
Every one of them renowned,
You took so many lions among men;
Yet now you shrink back,
Turning your neck as if to flee.
When truly challenged, she is your widow;
If you master yourself, she is your own wife,
Yet you stand afraid of a woman.
You babble, Kyyaz—
Whom do you think you are mocking?
You whimper, saying,
‘A woman slaughtered the wrestlers;
This is what a woman does when enraged,’
And you, warrior, turn soft.
If a woman frightens you so,
What will you do if bloodthirsty Semetey
Should suddenly return?
Can an enemy ever be spared?
If one of the tigers turns upon you,
Kyyaz, will begging save your life?
My friend, can these words be yours?
You have no spirit, Kyyaz;
You utter worthless talk
And take fright at a woman
As though the bloodthirsty khan had come.
At your side, Kyyaz,
Stands your champion, famed in battle,
Your bloodthirsty hero Kanchoro.
While your hero stands in fury,
What can happen to my hero Kyyaz?
Wretched Kyyaz, listen to my words:
Your Kanchoro is a black cliff
No goose could circle;
Your Kanchoro is a mountain
The lamenting people cannot cross.
I was a ravine and narrow pass
No one could advance against.
If blazing red embers come,
If fire comes upon you, brave Kyyaz,
If a deep-dug pit appears,
If danger overwhelms your fly-like soul,
From cruel slaughter and calamity,
From suffering sent by a khan,
I was the warrior who would turn it back.
Is it right, my friend brave Kyyaz,
For me to turn to the enemy?
Having delivered you to a madman,
Would I then split myself in two?
You speak on and on, Kyyaz,
And arrive at witless counsel,
Planting the worst thoughts—
Ah, you are a foolish Kyyaz.
You pretend to be wise.
Once Aichürök is taken as spoil,
For a month or two
She will rage and storm;
After many months have passed,
Once that woman has tasted meat,
She will make peace with you.
If you take Chürök as your wife,
Your wisdom will return when the day comes.
Do not overthink it;
Kyyaz, take my counsel,
Take a wife like Aichürök.
Who would not desire and love
Chürök, the peri’s daughter,
Such a radiant wonder!
If you desire dear Chürök,
Do not call her a wife, but a maiden,
That wonder whose path has been barred.
If fear of Chürök makes you hesitate,
Speak your mind more plainly;
If you will not take her, tell the truth!
For your sake, brave Kyyaz,
I made my quiver ready;
I destroyed Semetey,
My own kinsman.
I bound Khan Bakay,
And when he defied me,
I hewed the right shoulder
Of my own kinsman Külchoro.
You will never prosper, Kyyaz:
I have delivered the prize into your hands.
I settled and made Talas my home,
Placing greater hope in you alone,
Brave Kyyaz, than in my own kin.
Heed my words, Kyyaz;
Cease your foolish talk, Kyyaz!
I thought you were a true man, Kyyaz,
But you tremble for fear of a woman—
You are a witless child, Kyyaz!
I settled along the Six Rivers
And stood by you, accursed Kyyaz,
Thinking you closer than my father.
Let what has been said guide you;
Lion Kyyaz, heed my counsel.
Take that woman Aichürök,
That red-robed, slender-waisted,
Quivering infidel;
Reach out your cold hand
To that sly-tempered shrew,
That gleaming infidel,
That exceedingly beautiful woman,
And claim her as your prize.
My friend, move your people
From the land of the Seven Rivers,
Climb the mountain pass and settle there;
Take a fairy beauty and prosper yourself!
Recognize the wisdom in my words;
My warrior Kyyaz, heed my counsel.
We stirred the stars in the heavens;
We became friends unto the next world,
Chewing grains of white wheat,
Licking the edge of white steel,
Settling side by side,
And pledging ourselves for eternity.
Do not babble, Kyyaz;
When your turn comes, wield the hoe,
And if you have abundance, tend the people.
When were you ever brought low
By parting from elder or younger brother?!
Now is the time to slaughter and destroy your foes,
Now is the time for you to be mighty;
Fortune and prosperity have alighted on your head,
Now is the time to act.
Seize the village of that bloodthirsty bastard,
Tearing it down from the ridge,
And take his sun-faced wife!
Take the groves he planted in Talas;
Take the throne from which he ruled the people!
Leave my stepmother and take my sister-in-law;
Leave them both and take the one I offer.
Take his red-tailed camels;
Take his herds of every kind.
Brave Kyyaz, whose fortune has come from above,
Your lord has spoken—heed my counsel.
If Chürök agrees to the match,
Let us place authority in her hands
And make her a wise and honored wife.
If Chürök will not obey,
Strike her across the neck;
Do not leave the infidel alive,
But slaughter her for sport.
We shall seize her in the palace
And wreak boundless ruin;
Let us overpower and capture her
And bring disaster upon her.
The woman whose lord is dead,
The infidel fallen into your hands,
The woman whose husband is dead,
That frenzied infidel shrew—
Let us storm her palace
And scatter and exhaust together
Her countless goods and boundless wealth.
Let us plunder all there is to plunder
And firmly crush all resistance.
If Chürök struggles,
Let us offer her as a sacrifice.
Let us heap humiliation on her like sheep;
Let us cut off her head without mercy.
If the shrew refuses to see reason,
Let us be rid of that woman;
Let us massacre her people,
Bring misery upon their ruler,
And gather up the whole nation.
Of those older than seventeen,
Let us leave not one maiden,
And of those younger than thirty-three,
Let us leave not a single woman.
Let us spread savage calamity
And round them all up together;
Let us submit the many matrons and maidens
To the appraisers.
If Chürök turns away from us,
Let us kill her and not leave her alive,
And together bring about her end;
Then let us take another beautiful maiden
And enter the palace.
Let us make the revelry magnificent;
Let us find a wife among the maidens.
If Chürök remains stubborn,
We shall wage war without restraint.”
So Kanchoro spoke,
Addressing brave Kyyaz,
Like a lion whose words could not be contained.
Bridling and bristling with rage,
As though God had struck him mad once more,
Kanchoro sprang up in fury.
A thought came to him as he rose;
His face darkened beneath a cloud,
And his shout split the rocks.
He put his weapons in order
And girded on his unsheathed sword,
Like a cloud returning with rain,
Like a host marching to slaughter,
Like a champion who drinks blood,
Like a hero who will spare no one.
Rage seized him and his eyes blazed;
He ground his teeth with a crunch—
Such was the warrior you would have seen.
He seemed ready to settle along the blue hills;
Had you seen Kanchoro,
He looked ready to devour all before him,
As though he had occupied Chatkal.
If crossed, he seemed ready to flay a man alive;
He charged like a wild boar,
Raged like a tiger,
And none who fought him would survive.
He gathered himself like a champion,
And his muttering was like that of a demon;
The warrior’s fury
Was that of a wrestler who ruled a nation.
Whichever feature you observed,
He seemed a monster that swallowed men.
He broke away like a wolf,
As though ready to devour anyone who opposed him.
He was as slippery as a snake,
His strength like an unbroken cliff.
This ill-starred, cunning warrior
Seemed ready to swallow anyone who grappled with him.
He made every preparation,
Strapping on his battle-axe,
With the chest of a hungry lion
And the gaze of a hunting eagle.
To look upon Kanchoro’s bearing,
He was like a predator that could fell a bear,
Like a crag that could devour a full-grown camel—
Such was Kanchoro’s wrath.
At the frenzy of that ill-starred wretch,
Many stood dumbfounded,
